newsitem.title: USA: Clinton rushed to Washington for knee surgery.
newsitem.headline: Clinton rushed to Washington for knee surgery.

text.p: President Bill Clinton was rushed to Washington on Friday for surgery to repair a knee tendon torn in a late-night fall, vowing he still would fly to Finland for a summit with Russia's President Boris Yeltsin next week.
Doctors said Clinton, a hale and athletic man of 50, would make a full recovery but faced weeks of rehabilitation on crutches after relatively simple surgery.

The White House said he would be conscious under local anaesthetic during surgery, avoiding a temporary transfer of power to Vice President Al Gore, who himself suffered a leg injury two years ago that left him on crutches for weeks.
"He won't go under (a general anaesthetic)," spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn said in West Palm Beach, where Clinton was briefly hospitalized. "He'll be alert the whole time."
He is expected to have a form of local anaesthesia known as an epidural block, in the injured area.

Clinton, who stumbled on some "irregular shaped" steps about 1:20 A.M. EST (0620 GMT) on the Florida estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman, managed a wan smile for reporters as he was lifted in a wheelchair from a motorcade vehicle onto Air Force One for the flight to Washington.

The president flashed the thumbs-up sign when reporters asked how he felt as aides manhandled him backwards up the steps of the airplane in the wheelchair, his injured right leg immobilized and sticking straight out. "I feel good," he said.
He insisted he would proceed with a March 19-20 summit with Yeltsin in Helsinki, saying, "It will go on, you bet."
But aides were more circumspect. "We're going to wait and see how the surgery goes," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry.
The episode also cast doubt on Hillary Rodham Clinton's planned departure on Saturday for a two-week tour of six African nations. "We just don't know yet," said spokeswoman, Marsha Berry.

Clinton was due to undergo surgery at the National Naval Medical Centre in Bethesda, Maryland, a Washington suburb, around mid-day to repair a torn quadriceps tendon, which connects the kneecap to the upper thigh in his right leg.
Doctors at St Mary's Hospital in West Palm Beach where Clinton had X-rays said he would be expected to make a full recovery.
Dr. Joel Cohen, an orthopedic surgeon at the hospital, told reporters Clinton's leg would be immobilized in a brace and that he would be on crutches for several weeks.
Doctors said the injury was not uncommon and they described it as relatively minor.

"He has a tear in the quadriceps tendon," Cohen said at a press briefing. "It's not an uncommon injury. The expectation would be a return to full activity. They're going to sew the tendon back to his kneecap. He literally pulled the tendon from the bone," he said. "It was a deceleration injury."

Clinton's personal physician, U.S. Navy Captain Connie Mariano, said the president was in great pain after the fall, but had been given a non-narcotic anti-inflammatory painkiller and remained in good spirits.
"He remembers his right leg buckling out. He has a tear of the quadriceps tendon," Mariano said.
Glynn said Clinton stumbled on some steps while walking to his guest cottage on Norman's estate after staying up late chatting with the golfer following a political fund-raising dinner in the state.

Cohen said normally this kind of injury put the patient in a splint and on crutches for several weeks followed by a course of rehabilitation. He said full recovery could take between six weeks and three months.
Clinton was in Florida to play in a two-day golf tournament hosted by Norman beginning on Friday.
